chapters.voiceover: In 1853 a young lawyer named Paul Cornell bought three hundred acres of lakefront and named it Hyde Park, after the London park. The land was worthless until people could reach it. So Cornell handed the Illinois Central Railroad sixty acres, and in return he got a station at 53rd Street and six trains a day to downtown. Prairie became suburb. In 1857 he opened the Hyde Park House, a wood hotel on the water. Within ten years a thousand people lived here. By 1889 the township voted to join Chicago.

chapters.voiceover: In the summer of 1893, Jackson Park became a city made of plaster. The World's Columbian Exposition opened on May 1 and closed October 30, built to mark four hundred years since Columbus reached the Americas. Daniel Burnham ran construction. Frederick Law Olmsted turned a marshy lakefront into lagoons. The heart of it was the Court of Honor, white halls lit at night by electricity. People called it the White City. Roughly twenty-seven million came. Almost none was meant to last. Only the Palace of Fine Arts survived, reopening in 1933 as the Museum of Science and Industry.

chapters.voiceover: In 1889, John D. Rockefeller pledged six hundred thousand dollars toward a new Baptist university in Chicago, on one condition. Other donors had to match it. The University of Chicago was incorporated in 1890. Marshall Field gave the first ten acres in Hyde Park. To run it, Rockefeller picked William Rainey Harper, who had earned a Yale doctorate in his teens. Harper built a research university from nothing. The first classes met in 1892, five hundred ninety-four men and women. Henry Ives Cobb laid out the gray Gothic quadrangles that still stand.

chapters.voiceover: A single line in a property deed could decide who lived on a block. By 1940, about two hundred seventy-eight thousand Black Chicagoans lived in the city, up from roughly forty thousand in 1910. Most were held inside a narrow corridor on the South Side. The thing that held them was the racially restrictive covenant, a clause that barred sale or rent to anyone not white. Hyde Park and Woodlawn used them heavily, and the University of Chicago lent quiet support. The covenants did not fall until 1948, in Shelley v. Kraemer.

chapters.voiceover: In 1952 the University of Chicago organized the South East Chicago Commission to remake the streets around its campus. The renewal plan covered eight hundred fifty-six acres and called for tearing down six hundred thirty-eight buildings. The first came down in 1955. The City Council approved the plan in 1958. About four thousand families were displaced. The university spent twenty-nine million dollars of its own money to buy and rebuild the neighborhood. Who got to come back was not random. Hyde Park's Black population fell by about forty percent. Then the university turned toward Woodlawn.
